access.fees: $82/person climbing registration, required year-round for any travel above 10,000 ft or onto a glacier, plus a $12/person/night wilderness permit for overnight camping (charged May 1-Sep 15 only); park entrance is $30/vehicle for 7 days.
access.notes: How to get it: pay online in advance (pay.gov / recreation.gov), then register in person. Winter (Sept 16–May 21): self-issue at the Paradise Old Station kiosk after paying online. Summer (May 22–Sept 30): no self-issue — register at a Wilderness Information Center (Longmire, Paradise, or White River); roughly half of summer registration slots are held for walk-up, up to 24 hrs ahead. No timed-entry vehicle reservation is in effect for the 2026 season, so park entry itself is first-come, first-served.
access.rules: Camp only at designated Summerland-area wilderness sites; stay on the maintained trail through the fragile Summerland meadow; pack out human waste above the toilets (required for high camps and glacier travel).
access.permit: Climbing registration required for all travel above 10,000 ft or on any glacier (pay the $82 climbing fee online first; in summer, registration is done in person at a wilderness information center, and self-registration is available only in winter); a separate wilderness permit is required for overnight camping at Summerland or the high camp — reserve ahead or get a walk-up permit at a wilderness information center within 24 hrs of your trip during the May 22-Sep 30 walk-up season.
access.closures: The Sunrise/White River Road is snow-gated and typically doesn't open until late June-early July; it closes for the season by mid-October, with nightly gate closures at the White River Campground junction beginning in late September. Check the NPS road-status page before driving up.
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful / interagency annual pass covers only the $30 vehicle entrance fee — it does NOT cover the separate $82 climbing registration fee.

overnight_permit.what: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, plus climbing registration and fee for the glaciers
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov or get a walk-up permit at the White River Wilderness Information Center; register and pay the climbing fee before the climb.

approach: From the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead (3,800 ft) on the Sunrise/White River Road (WA-410), follow the Wonderland Trail south along Fryingpan Creek about 4.5 mi to Summerland (~5,900-5,950 ft), a subalpine meadow with a stock/hiker shelter and toilet. Leave the maintained trail there and climb north of Meany Crest across the Meany snowfield, making a rising traverse toward rock outcrops around 7,000-7,350 ft — the standard high camp. From camp, gain the Fryingpan Glacier, rope up, and traverse southwest to 9,100 ft Whitman Notch for the first view of the Whitman Glacier, then cross the upper Whitman Glacier to the peak's high shoulder before the final steep snow couloir and Class 3-4 summit block.

access.fees: $82/person climbing registration, required year-round for any travel above 10,000 ft or onto a glacier, plus a $12/person/night wilderness permit for overnight camping (May 1-Sep 15); park entrance is $30/vehicle for 7 days.
access.notes: Inside the national park, so a Northwest Forest Pass does not apply; the park entrance fee does. Climbing registration and the per-person climbing fee are required before going onto a glacier or above 10,000 ft.
access.rules: Blue bags required for human waste above high camp — pack out and deposit only in barrels marked "Human Waste" at Camp Muir or the trailhead; do not cache on-route. Check-out is required after every climb.
access.permit: Climbing registration required for all travel above 10,000 ft or on any glacier; a separate wilderness permit is required for overnight camping at Summerland or high camp.
access.closures: The road is usually open past the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead to the White River Campground lot by mid-to-late May; the upper road to Sunrise stays snow-gated until late June-early July and closes for the season by mid-October.
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful / interagency annual pass covers only the $30 vehicle entrance fee, not the separate $82 climbing registration fee.

overnight_permit.what: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, plus climbing registration and fee for the glaciers
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov or get a walk-up permit at the White River Wilderness Information Center; register and pay the climbing fee before the climb.

approach: Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead (~3,800-3,900 ft) on the Sunrise/White River Road, about 3 miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed Fryingpan Creek Trail, which climbs gently along Fryingpan Creek through old-growth forest. At roughly 3.2 miles / ~1,400 ft of gain (about 2-2.5 hrs from the car) the trail reaches an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek - the main water source and a spot that can require careful footing in high runoff. Continue up-trail toward Summerland, reaching that popular alpine backcountry camp (patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, wilderness permit required to camp) at about 4.5 miles and roughly 2,500 ft gain (~5,900 ft elevation) - this is the last reliable running water before the climb proper. From Summerland, leave the maintained trail and pick up the climbers' 'spring route' path that heads northwest of the campground knoll, ascending steep tundra/snow up the Meany Snowfield toward Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft that serves as the standard high camp (flat tent sites, stone wind breaks). This band between Summerland and Meany Crest is where route-finding matters most: parties that contour too far climber's right have gotten cliffed out in a bowl below rock bands, so stick to the cairned/bootpacked line. Above Meany Crest, gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier - rope up here, as this begins sustained glacier travel with real crevasse hazard - and climb generally south/southwest across the lower glacier apron to the broad notch separating the Fryingpan and Whitman Glaciers (~9,000-9,100 ft, commonly called Whitman Notch). From the notch, traverse and climb the upper Whitman Glacier, crossing a bergschrund (usually a straightforward step-across early season, wider and trickier late season) up moderate glacier slopes to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to a loose rock-and-scree gully. Climb the gully to a short (~6 ft) headwall step, then a gully-chimney to the summit notch, finishing with an exposed, loose Class 3 scramble (roughly 30-100 ft) along a narrow, crumbly andesite ridge crest to the 11,138 ft summit - there is major exposure here, with a roughly 2,000 ft drop to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. Additional hazards along the whole approach: avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft/early-season conditions, and afternoon whiteout or thunderstorm activity common on Rainier's flanks.

Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road (or, when the road is snowed in, at the year-round Narada Falls lot). Take the signed Pinnacle Peak Trail from the south side of the road; it climbs steadily through forest and subalpine meadow for about 1.3 miles and 1,050 ft of gain to the 5,920-ft saddle just south of Pinnacle Peak. From the saddle, instead of continuing up Pinnacle, traverse climber's-left (east) across Pinnacle's south-facing scree/boulder field, staying around 6,000-6,200 ft, to the col between Pinnacle and Castle — roughly another half mile of cross-country travel to the base of Castle's south/southeast side.

Same as the Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes (4,859 ft), take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the Pinnacle–Plummer saddle, then contour across Pinnacle's south-face scree/talus to the base of Castle's southeast side and scramble up broken ground to reach the base of the summit block.

road.name: Teanaway Road (N. Fork Teanaway River Rd, paved to ~29 Pines Campground) to gravel FR-9737, then FR-9737-112 (Beverly Creek Road)
road.status: Gravel and summer-passable in normal years, but the FR-9737-112 spur and trailhead are currently under an active USFS closure (Labor Mountain Fire damage, through Dec 31, 2026)
road.driveNote: Final mile-plus on FR-9737-112 is a rough one-lane road with brush close on both sides; high clearance recommended. Turn right onto FR-9737-112 just before the road would cross Beverly Creek.
road.seasonalGate: Snow closure in winter/spring; additionally closed in 2026 due to Labor Mountain Fire damage

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/annual) required at the trailhead
access.rules: Leave No Trace; Alpine Lakes Wilderness group-size and camping rules apply on the upper mountain
access.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead signboard where the route crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary; no day-use quota
access.closures: ACTIVE CLOSURE as of 2026: Beverly Creek Road (FSR 9737-112), Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, and Bean Creek Trail #1391.1/.2 — the entire standard approach to Earl Peak — are closed under a USFS fire-damage closure order tied to the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire (~43,000 acres, Cle Elum/Wenatchee River Ranger Districts). The order is in effect through Dec 31, 2026; confirm current status with Cle Elum Ranger District before heading out. Beyond the fire closure, Teanaway roads are also snow-gated in winter/spring.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Cle Elum Ranger District

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk. This is distinct from the quota Enchantment Permit Area to the west.

approach: Start at the Stafford Creek Trailhead (Trail #1359), Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, at the end of Stafford Creek Road (FR 9703), which leaves North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) past 29 Pines Campground — a small, often-overflowing lot for roughly 20 cars (Northwest Forest Pass required). From the trailhead, Stafford Creek Trail #1359 climbs at a gentle-to-moderate grade through dry ponderosa/lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek for the first mile (a short rerouted, steeper switchback section around 0.5 mile bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread). The trail continues gaining gradually along the creek — figure roughly 3,000 ft of gain spread over the approach — reaching a signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) at about 3.5–3.8 miles; this crossing of Stafford Creek is the last reliable, easy water source before the high country and is worth topping off here. Bear right (east/north) at the junction to stay on the Navaho Pass approach. Around 4.5 miles the trail opens into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with established campsites and a feeder stream — the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days, and another water source. Beyond camp the trail crosses the barren, eroded 'Moon Landing' stretch (sparse vegetation, serpentine/greenstone talus) before a final push to Navaho Pass (~6,000 ft) around mile 5.5. A commonly used shortcut leaves the main trail where two creek forks merge around the 3-mile mark, climbing steep, loose slopes directly up the northeast-facing drainage to the col below Navaho's southeast ridge — it saves close to 2 miles of trail hiking but is steeper, unmaintained, and involves loose scree/dirt, so most parties use it only for one direction of the trip. Total car-to-summit is on the order of 11–13 miles round trip with about 4,000–4,200 ft of gain depending on which junction/shortcut combination is used. Note: as of 2026 this trail corridor has had closures tied to Labor Mountain Fire and storm damage — verify current Forest Service trail status before heading in. A second off-trail variant leaves the trail right after the Stafford Creek crossing and climbs directly into the open bowl between Earl Peak and Navaho Peak to about 5,000 ft, scrambles north to the ridgeline near 6,000 ft, then follows the west/southwest ridge to the summit — a different line than the northeast-drainage shortcut.

road.name: Smithbrook Road (FR 6700)
road.status: Closed to vehicles (storm damage) under an order effective May 20, 2026 through December 31, 2027 unless lifted sooner; confirm current status before driving.
road.driveNote: Normally gravel off US-2 east of Stevens Pass to the trailhead (~4,000 ft), but FR 6700 has been closed to vehicles since a Forest Service order (effective May 20, 2026) covering storm-damaged Wenatchee River Ranger District roads after Dec 2025 storms.
road.seasonalGate: Currently closed by storm-damage order, not just seasonal snow-gating; historically also snow-gated in winter.
